international.headline: When the whole world had inflation, America had slightly less than average. Now that the world doesn't, America has more.

assumptions: Advanced economies were exposed to the same global supply, energy and reopening shocks, so peer inflation is a reasonable counterfactual for the non-domestic component.
The gap between US and peer inflation is treated as the domestically-driven part. This is an approximation, not an identification strategy.
caveats: US CPI and euro-area HICP are built differently. US CPI includes owners' equivalent rent at ~24% of the basket; HICP excludes owner-occupied housing entirely. On a harmonized basis the US 2022 peak was 10.1%, not the 9.1% usually quoted -- roughly two-thirds of the apparent US-vs-Europe gap at the peak is measurement.
The peer group is European because FRED's OECD-sourced series for the UK, Canada and Japan are stale (ending 2020, 2025 and 2021). This is not a full G7 comparison and should not be described as one.

Europe's energy exposure in 2022 was larger than America's -- the euro-area basket is ~1.6x more energy-weighted and it absorbed a gas shock roughly eight times larger in level terms. That cuts against reading the 2022 gap as pure US outperformance.
October 2025 US CPI does not exist; the shutdown meant it was never collected.
falsifiers: If the US-minus-peer gap were similar across all administrations, it would carry no information about policy.
If the gap disappeared using a different peer group or a harmonized US measure, the finding would be an artefact of index construction.

items.name: Ground beef
items.note: per lb. Cattle herd at multi-decade lows plus tariffs on imported beef.

items.name: Eggs
items.note: grade A large, per dozen. The 2022-25 spike was avian influenza, not policy -- and the subsequent fall is real. We say so.

sample.source: BLS average price data via FRED

assumptions: Terms are compared on ANNUALISED rates because they are different lengths (48 months vs ~18). Raw totals would favour the longer term.
Average price series are not seasonally adjusted; annualised rates over multi-year spans are not materially affected by this.
caveats: The 2022-25 egg spike was highly pathogenic avian influenza, not economic policy -- and the subsequent decline is real. Both are shown.
Beef prices also reflect a US cattle herd at multi-decade lows, a supply cycle that began before 2025.
Coffee, bananas and cocoa are import-dependent and weather-exposed; tariffs are one input among several.
falsifiers: If most staples were rising more slowly now than in the previous term, the claim of accelerating grocery inflation would fail.
If the acceleration were confined to items with known idiosyncratic supply shocks (eggs, beef), it could not be attributed to policy.

assumptions: Monthly change in total nonfarm payrolls is the standard headline measure of job creation.
caveats: October 2025 payrolls are depressed by the 43-day federal shutdown itself, not only by underlying conditions.
Powell noted in December 2025 that the birth-death model may OVERSTATE payroll growth by ~60,000/month -- a bias that flatters recent numbers, not the reverse.
Payroll figures are revised for two months after first publication; recent months are provisional.
Initial claims and the unemployment rate remain historically low. Both are shown.
falsifiers: If average monthly payroll growth in the current term matched the previous term, the slowdown claim would fail.
If the negative months were confined to the shutdown period, they could not be read as a broader trend.

verdict.plain_english: Headline inflation is 3.36% but median inflation is 2.69%. Broad, demand-driven inflation raises the median. This did not -- the overshoot is concentrated in a few categories.

sample.source: BLS and Cleveland Fed via FRED

assumptions: Median and trimmed-mean CPI (Cleveland Fed) are standard tools for separating relative-price shocks from broad-based inflation.
caveats: Core PCE exceeded core CPI in mid-2026 -- an inversion of the usual relationship. The largest supercore contributor is an imputed portfolio-management fee that tracks equity prices and has no CPI counterpart. We report CPI-based measures and say so.
October 2025 is missing from every CPI-derived series: the shutdown meant it was never collected and it cannot be recovered.
falsifiers: If median and trimmed-mean CPI had risen with headline, the shock would be broad-based and an energy-specific explanation would fail.
If the headline-median gap were within normal historical variation, the chart would show nothing.

rows.name: Median CPI (Cleveland Fed)
rows.note: THE breadth test. Broad monetary inflation raises the median. It didn't move.

rows.name: Median real weekly earnings
rows.note: Median rather than average -- the mean is pulled by the top of the distribution and is not what a typical worker experiences.

rows.name: Labor share of income
rows.note: 53.7% in Q1 2026 -- lowest since the series began in 1947.

rows.name: S&P 500
rows.note: Genuinely up. Concede it plainly -- a scorecard that hides the opposing rows is not a scorecard.

rows.name: Consumer sentiment
rows.note: Has become politically polarised since 2020; respondents' partisanship predicts their answer. Flag this rather than leaning on it.

rows.name: Unit labor costs
rows.note: +0.5% y/y -- consistent with inflation BELOW 2%. Kills the wage-price-spiral story.

rows.name: Personal saving rate
rows.note: 2.7% in June 2026, a two-decade low, down from 5.5% in April 2025. Households are covering higher prices by saving less.

rows.name: Long-term unemployed share
rows.note: 27.3% of the unemployed have been jobless 27+ weeks, up from 21.1% in January 2025. Hiring is frozen even though layoffs are low.

sample.source: BLS, BEA, Federal Reserve via FRED

assumptions: Terms compared on annualised rates of change, not levels.
'Better' and 'worse' are from a household's point of view, which is stated per row rather than assumed.
caveats: Consumer sentiment has been strongly polarised by respondent party since 2020 and should not be read as a clean welfare measure.
Quarterly series (GDP, labor share, unit labor costs) lag the monthly ones; end dates differ by row and are shown.
Equity prices and initial claims are genuinely favourable. They are included for that reason.
falsifiers: If most household-facing indicators had improved, the central claim would fail.
If the deterioration were confined to volatile series while broad measures improved, the picture would be mixed rather than negative.

events.label: US and Israel strike Iran; Strait of Hormuz closes
Two-week ceasefire agreed; Hormuz reopens partially
60-day ceasefire and US-Iran Memorandum of Understanding
US strikes Iran again; the ceasefire is declared over
Attacks on Saudi tankers; war risk premiums hit 7.5-10% of hull value
Escalation threats push Brent back above $90
US and Iran trade strikes in the strait; the August lull ends

assumptions: Event signs (+1 escalation, -1 de-escalation) were assigned in data/war_milestones.json before this test was run.
Under the null that war news does not move oil prices, each event matching its sign is a coin flip.
caveats: Six events are not six independent draws -- they are sequential moves in one conflict.
The event list is editorial, compiled from news reporting, not machine-generated.
Windows were fixed in advance at [-1,+5]; the two alternatives are reported rather than selected from.
falsifiers: If prices had risen on de-escalation events, or failed to fall on ceasefires, the war-attribution claim would fail outright.
If matches were at chance (about 3 of 6), there would be no signal.

electricity_kwh_per_household_month: 855.0 kwh -- EIA Residential Energy Consumption Survey, US average
caveats: Cumulative cost assumes the current monthly gap applied evenly since the baseline. Prices moved through that window -- notably falling back during the June 2026 ceasefire -- so this is an approximation.
The grocery line uses the MEDIAN move across tracked staples, which is deliberately conservative: it ignores the largest increases.
Household consumption varies enormously. These are national averages and every one of them is adjustable.
falsifiers: If the tracked prices had not risen since the baseline, the receipt would total zero.

chains.title: From Qatar's gas to next year's food
chains.preface: Qatar's Ras Laffan LNG complex was damaged in the war and will take three to five years to repair. That is a context figure, not a FRED series, so this chain starts at the European gas price it moved.

edges.note: pre-war sample; a 1% move in the upstream series is associated with a 0.30% long-run move in the downstream one

assumptions: Each link is a reduced-form pass-through from the upstream series to the downstream one, estimated on pre-war data and applied to the episode.
12-month changes for monthly indices are by calendar month (October 2025 is a gap); weekly and daily series use the nearest print a year earlier.
caveats: Elasticities are conditional associations, not structural parameters; other inputs (wages, weather, tariffs) move these prices too.
The fertiliser chain starts at the European gas price; the Qatari outage that moved it is a context figure, not a series.
Producer price indexes lag retail by a month or more; the chain is drawn in causal order, not in the order the data arrives.
falsifiers: If an estimated long-run elasticity were indistinguishable from zero, that link would not carry the shock and the chain would break there.
If a downstream node moved before its upstream node during the war, the stated direction would be wrong.

assumptions: Terms are compared on ANNUALISED rates because they are different lengths. Raw totals would favour longer terms.
A term is attributed the change that occurred during it. This is a convention, not a causal claim.
caveats: Presidents do not control the economy on a four-year clock. Every term here inherited conditions and encountered shocks it did not cause -- each row carries that context and it should be read.
The current term is incomplete and is excluded from rankings.
Party averages are means over a handful of terms and are dominated by whichever administration happened to meet a recession.
Economic policy acts with long and variable lags; effects often land in a successor's term.
falsifiers: If the ordering flipped when the metric or the window changed, no stable party-level difference would exist.
If terms that encountered recessions accounted for the entire party gap, the gap would be about timing, not policy.

falsifiers: If the ordering flipped when the metric or the window changed, no stable party-level difference would exist.
If terms that encountered recessions accounted for the entire party gap, the gap would be about timing, not policy.

terms.label: Trump I
terms.context: Ended with the COVID-19 shock; unemployment hit 14.8% in April 2020.

terms.label: Biden
terms.context: Inherited the COVID reopening; global supply-chain and energy shocks drove a worldwide inflation surge, peaking 9.1% June 2022.

terms.label: Trump II
terms.context: 2026 tariffs; the Iran war from February 2026 took oil from $57 to $114.

none.label: As measured
none.note: Inauguration to inauguration, every month counted.

ex_covid.label: Excluding COVID
ex_covid.note: Drops 2020-03 to 2021-06. Removes both the 2020 collapse and the reopening surge, which land in different administrations and distort them in opposite directions.

ex_recession.label: Excluding recessions
ex_recession.note: Drops every NBER-dated recession month, applied equally to all terms. Tests whether a party gap is really about which administrations met downturns.

lag12.label: 12-month policy lag
lag12.note: Credits each term's first 12 months to its predecessor. Economic policy acts with long and variable lags; this is a crude but transparent way to stop giving a president credit for their first year.

assumptions: Terms are compared on ANNUALISED rates because they are different lengths. Raw totals would favour longer terms.
A term is attributed the change that occurred during it. This is a convention, not a causal claim.
caveats: Presidents do not control the economy on a four-year clock. Every term here inherited conditions and encountered shocks it did not cause -- each row carries that context and it should be read.
The current term is incomplete and is excluded from rankings.
Party averages are means over a handful of terms and are dominated by whichever administration happened to meet a recession.
Economic policy acts with long and variable lags; effects often land in a successor's term.
falsifiers: If the ordering flipped when the metric or the window changed, no stable party-level difference would exist.
If terms that encountered recessions accounted for the entire party gap, the gap would be about timing, not policy.

crude_daily.name: WTI Crude, Cushing spot
crude_daily.note: Cushing SPOT, not front-month futures. Press figures for 8 Jul 2026 quote $73.52 from the futures contract; spot closed $74.56. Both are correct and they are different instruments -- do not mix them on one chart. The spot peak is $114.58 on 7 Apr 2026, the day the first ceasefire was announced; an earlier version of the page quoted $114.01 on 6 Apr, which is the previous day's close.

hormuz_transits.name: Strait of Hormuz
hormuz_transits.source: IMF PortWatch (IMF / University of Oxford), AIS-based estimates
hormuz_transits.note: Estimated from satellite AIS positions. Vessels transmitting no position are not counted, so this is a floor on traffic, not a census -- and it is not a queue count. Recent days are revised as late AIS data arrives.

war_milestones.headline: Iran nuclear talks collapse; Gulf posturing begins
war_milestones.description: Breakdown of nuclear negotiations leads to increased military posturing in the Persian Gulf. Oil markets begin pricing supply risk - though WTI is still near a 12-month low of $57 and had fallen roughly 20% over 2025.

war_milestones.headline: Supreme Court strikes down the IEEPA tariffs, 6-3
war_milestones.description: Learning Resources v. Trump holds that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act does not authorize tariffs. Collection ends February 24. Average import tariffs fall roughly 4.8 percentage points - eight days before the Iran strikes.

war_milestones.headline: Section 122 blanket 10% surcharge replaces the struck-down tariffs
war_milestones.description: Proclamation 11012 imposes a 10 percent ad valorem surcharge on roughly $1.0 trillion of imports. Energy and energy products are exempted verbatim. The surcharge expires by statute on July 24, 2026.

war_milestones.headline: US and Israel strike Iran; Strait of Hormuz closes
war_milestones.description: Coordinated strikes begin. The IRGC declares the Strait of Hormuz closed within days, removing roughly 13.8 million barrels per day of gross transit - about 20 percent of world oil trade. WTI begins a five-week climb from $67 to $114.

war_milestones.headline: Platts suspends all Hormuz-transiting grades from the Dubai benchmark
war_milestones.description: The price reporting agency cuts deliverable grades from five to two, leaving only Murban (loading ex-Fujairah) and Oman. The Dubai benchmark after this date measures a structurally different basket than before it.

war_milestones.headline: IEA members agree to release 400 million barrels
war_milestones.description: The largest coordinated release in the agency's 52-year history - roughly one third of government stockpiles across 32 nations. The US share is 172 million barrels over about 120 days. Expert estimates put the short-term price effect near $2 per barrel.

war_milestones.headline: Two-week ceasefire agreed; Hormuz reopens partially
war_milestones.description: The US and Iran agree to a two-week ceasefire including reopening of the Strait. Oil plunges below $100 from its $114 peak.

war_milestones.headline: Physical crude trades $35 above paper - a record
war_milestones.description: North Sea Dated commands a record $35 per barrel premium over ICE Brent futures. April's Dated range spans roughly $50 intramonth, the widest ever recorded. The premium collapses to $3 by early May.

war_milestones.headline: 60-day ceasefire and US-Iran Memorandum of Understanding
war_milestones.description: Vessels transiting the Strait must coordinate with Iran's newly established Persian Gulf Strait Authority. Transits triple within days; Hormuz oil flow recovers to about 4.8 million barrels per day. WTI falls all the way back to $69.74 - below its pre-war level.

war_milestones.headline: US strikes Iran again; the ceasefire is declared over
war_milestones.description: Retaliation for attacks on three commercial ships in the Strait. WTI rises 4.4 percent to $73.52 and Brent 5.2 percent to $78.02 on the day.

war_milestones.headline: Three tankers attacked in a single day; a seafarer killed
war_milestones.description: Stolt Magnesium, Mombasa B and Al Bahyah are struck in and around the strait. One crew member is killed on Mombasa B and eight injured. The IRGC says it targeted vessels using mined routes.

war_milestones.headline: Trump imposes 50% Section 338 tariffs on Canadian vehicles, alcohol and dairy
war_milestones.description: Three proclamations under the 1930 Tariff Act, covering about C$27.6 billion of Canadian exports; energy, potash and Section 232 goods excluded. The White House says the duties apply regardless of USMCA origin and that the agreement will not be renewed in its current form.

war_milestones.headline: Attacks on Saudi tankers; war risk premiums hit 7.5-10% of hull value
war_milestones.description: Marsh reports war risk insurance at 7.5 to 10 percent of hull value for a single transit, up from 1 to 3 percent weeks earlier and 0.25 percent before the war. On a $100 million tanker that is $7.5-10 million per voyage.

war_milestones.headline: Section 122 surcharge expires; Section 301 becomes the baseline
war_milestones.description: The 10 percent blanket surcharge lapses by statute after 150 days. Section 301 forced-labor tariffs at 10 and 12.5 percent across roughly 99 percent of imports become the operative regime.

war_milestones.headline: Escalation threats push Brent back above $90
war_milestones.description: Renewed threats against Iran drive Brent above $90 as tanker attacks in the Strait continue and fighting spreads toward the Red Sea.

war_milestones.headline: A month-long lull in US-Iran strikes begins; attacks on merchant ships continue
war_milestones.description: No large US or Iranian military exchanges for the month. Thirteen commercial vessels are nonetheless struck in August. The strait stays effectively closed: IMF PortWatch counts single-digit daily transits against a pre-war average of about 83.

war_milestones.headline: Strategic Petroleum Reserve falls below 300 million barrels, lowest since 1983
war_milestones.description: Emergency releases to hold prices down have drawn the reserve to its lowest level in more than forty years. EIA weekly stocks read 286.6 million barrels by 28 August.

war_milestones.headline: July CPI: 3.4% headline, 2.5% core, energy +14.7%
war_milestones.description: Headline and core both ease a tenth from June. Energy falls 1.5% on the month but remains 14.7% above a year earlier. The breadth test still reads as a tail shock: median CPI 2.7%.

war_milestones.headline: IEA: Gulf exports down 2.1 mb/d; world supply to fall 4.3 mb/d in 2026
war_milestones.description: The August Oil Market Report says the strait was 'effectively closed again in early July'. Observed stocks have drawn 410 million barrels since February. World demand is now forecast to fall 1.6 mb/d this year.

war_milestones.headline: MV Minoan Dignity struck, one crew killed, on the day the President says the strait is 'open and operating'
war_milestones.description: The bulk carrier is abandoned after an Iranian strike. Lloyd's List Intelligence counts about 14 non-Iranian transits a day that week against roughly 100 before the war.

war_milestones.headline: Section 338 tariffs on Canada take effect after talks collapse
war_milestones.description: A three-day pause for negotiations ends without a deal; Prime Minister Carney recalls Canada's negotiators. The 50% duties enter into force at 12:01 a.m.

war_milestones.headline: US Navy says it has cleared mines from the strait
war_milestones.description: Officials confirm underwater drones identified more than 100 suspected mines. Transits do not recover: PortWatch counts four vessels that day.

war_milestones.headline: Trump announces a deal with Caracas to refill the SPR with Venezuelan crude
war_milestones.description: Announced as the reserve sits at a 44-year low. No volumes or dates published.

war_milestones.headline: Saudi tanker Sidr struck; two crew killed. Thirteen merchant ships hit in August
war_milestones.description: The deadliest attack of the month closes it. WTI ends August at $87.03, up from $69.74 at the July ceasefire low.

war_milestones.headline: US and Iran trade strikes in the strait; the August lull ends
war_milestones.description: Renewed exchanges after a month of quiet. WTI spot closes $91.48, up 5.1% on the day; Brent $96.02. Event added on 5 September 2026 with the price path already visible -- the sign is theory-driven (escalation raises prices) but this event is not pre-registered in the way the first six were.

war_milestones.headline: Dutch central bank confirms it moved 86 tonnes of gold out of New York and Ottawa
war_milestones.description: De Nederlandsche Bank cites 'increasing geopolitical unrest'. New York's share of Dutch reserves falls from 31% to 18.5%. The Fed's own custody table shows foreign gold under earmark down about 160 tonnes since August 2025.

war_milestones.headline: August payrolls +162,000, the best month in five; long-term unemployed 27%
war_milestones.description: Well above the 53,000 consensus. Unemployment 4.1%. One strong month lifts the term average to about 42,000 a month against 321,000 in the previous term. Hires rate 3.2%, quits 1.9%: still low-fire, low-hire.

war_milestones.headline: Canada's dollar-for-dollar counter-tariffs take effect on C$27.6 billion of US goods
war_milestones.description: Steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, electronics. Carney: talks will not resume until the US changes its approach.

It also reports official Treasury custody at the New York Fed fell USD 82bn to USD 2.7tn in March 2026 as some central banks sold to defend their currencies after the war began.

fed_counterpoint.name: Why gold did not actually overtake Treasuries as the world's favourite reserve asset
fed_counterpoint.author: Colin Weiss, Federal Reserve Board
fed_counterpoint.finding: The crossover is a valuation effect driven by private ETF demand since late 2024, not central bank accumulation; by June 2026 foreign official Treasury holdings again exceeded world gold reserves excluding the US in dollar terms. Five legacy holders (US, Germany, Italy, France, IMF) own 52% of official gold and have not added since the 1970s. Foreign officials bought roughly USD 200bn of Treasuries net between 2022 and April 2026.

bases.note: Iran struck the Navy's Bahrain logistics hub on the first day. Regional ports large enough for a carrier remain inside missile range, so supply ships sail to Diego Garcia and the fleet resupplies at sea every five to six days. USS Abraham Lincoln spent about nine months deployed without a port call before USS George Washington relieved it on 20 August.

munitions.note: CSIS estimated roughly a third of Patriot interceptors remained as of 27 July and that rebuilding to pre-war levels would take at least three years. CNN reported about 80% of THAAD and half of Patriot stocks used. The $21bn munitions line in the supplemental is consistent with the estimates the Secretary disputes.
